en.Die (un)berechtigte Furcht vor Kriminali: The (Un)warranted Fear of Crime in Germany
en.Registrierte Kriminalität, Strafverfolgu: Recorded crime, law enforcement and the public's sense of safety — for Germany as a whole and for each federal state.
en.Registrierte Straftaten je 100.000 Einwo: Recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants in 2025. Dividing by population makes states of different size comparable. The count covers what came to police attention — not what actually happened.
en.Anteil der Befragten, die sich nachts im: Share of respondents who feel unsafe walking alone in their local area after dark. From the European Social Survey (rounds 1–11, 2002–2023, Germany, weighted). Between 121 and 3,332 respondents per state; states below 300 are shown in grey.
en.Anteil der registrierten Fälle, die die: Share of recorded cases that police report as cleared (2025). A high rate does not mean little crime: it can also mean that more easily solved cases are reported.
en.Bruttoinlandsprodukt je Einwohner in Eur: Gross domestic product per capita in euros (2024), Working Group on National Accounts of the Länder. A measure of economic output, not of household income.
en.Anteil der registrierten Arbeitslosen an: Share of registered unemployed among the labour force (2025), statistics of the Federal Employment Agency. Relative to all civilian labour force participants.
en.Anteil der Bevölkerung mit Migrationshin: Share of the population with a migration background (microcensus). Includes naturalised Germans, ethnic German resettlers and their descendants — hence higher than the share of foreign nationals.
en.Anteil der Personen ohne deutsche Staats: Share of persons without German citizenship (2022 census). Citizenship only, not origin. Well below the migration-background share.
en.Einwohner je Quadratkilometer, berechnet: Inhabitants per square kilometre, computed from population and area (2025). A measure of settlement density — city-states are several times higher than territorial states.
en.Registrierte Fälle je 100.000 Einwohner: Recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants. 2025. National average: 6,600.
en.Anteil der Fälle, in denen mindestens ei: Share of cases in which at least one suspect was identified, 2025, national average: 57.9 %.
en.Anteil, der sich nachts beim Alleingehen: Share who feel unsafe walking alone after dark (ESS, rounds 5–11 pooled). Grey bars: too few respondents for reliable statements.
en.Erfasste Fälle 1987–2025. Langfristig rü: Recorded cases 1987–2025. Declining in the long run, volatile in the short run.
en.ESS 2002–2023 (Deutschland fehlt in Rund: ESS 2002–2023 (Germany missing in round 10/2020; interpolated, shown dotted).
en.Zwei Zahlen, die weit auseinanderlaufen:: Two figures moving apart: total offences have more than doubled since 2016, while violent offences stayed essentially flat. A large share of the cases are propaganda offences. Note: the six panels use different scales — line heights are comparable only within a panel.
en.Je Phänomenbereich ein eigenes Feld mit: One panel per category, each with its own scale. Comparisons run within a panel: offences classified as right-wing rose from 23,555 to 42,544, left-wing climbed to 13,490 in 2025. Violent offences (dotted) are flatter — case numbers grow mainly in propaganda offences, not in violence. In each panel the left axis shows all offences, the right axis violent offences on their own scale; the panels themselves are scaled differently. What can be compared are the trends, not the heights.
en.Anteil mit Unsicherheitsgefühl je Alters: Share feeling unsafe by age group. The ♀/♂ symbol marks gender, the colour the migration background. The pale line is a moving regression over all individuals, not over the seven points. Each group rests on at least 88 respondents (median 975); the case count appears on hover.
en.Die Furcht vor einem Delikt (dunkel) und: Fear of an offence (dark) against the perceived likelihood of becoming a victim (gold). Online fraud leads by a wide margin, and for every offence fear exceeds the assumed probability.
en.Anteil der Menschen, die sich an einem O: Share of people who feel safe in a given place — by day and by night. At night the sense of safety collapses everywhere, most sharply at railway stations and in parks.
en.Anteil „beunruhigt“ je Delikt, SKiD 2020: Share feeling worried, by offence, SKiD 2020 and 2024.
en.Registrierte Fälle, aufgeklärte Fälle un: Recorded cases, cleared cases and convictions compared
en.Registrierte Fälle je 100.000 Einwohner,: Recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants, Germany against the median of around 40 comparison countries. The vertical gap between the lines shows whether Germany sits above or below the European middle. For assault and theft Germany is several times higher, for residential burglary roughly level. The series starts in 2009: for 2008 Eurostat reports a multiple of the following year for assault and theft — a break in the series, not a real decline. Each panel has its own scale.

en.Anteil jedes Phänomenbereichs am Gesamta: Share of each category in the total, 2016 to 2025. Using shares puts all categories on one scale; in absolute counts the small categories would vanish next to right-wing offences. The dashed line shows violent offences, measured against the same total. A falling share does not mean falling case numbers: the total rose from 41,549 cases (2016) to 85,837 (2025).
en.Einordnung: Das Gesamtaufkommen ist von: Reading: total offences rose from 41,549 cases (2016) to 85,837 (2025), an increase of 107 per cent. Politically motivated violent offences stayed essentially flat over the same period (4,311 against 4,156 cases, −3.6 per cent); their share of the total therefore fell from 10.4 to 4.8 per cent. A large part of the cases are propaganda offences: 35.4 per cent in 2025. Interpretation: in absolute counts the right-wing category grew from 23,555 to 42,544 (+81 per cent) and the left-wing category from 9,389 to 13,490 (+44 per cent). The residual category — cases not attributed to any ideology — grew from 5,233 to 20,934 and was temporarily the largest single group: in 2022 it stood at 40.9 per cent, ahead of the right-wing category (39.9 per cent). Limits: for 2016 foreign and religious ideology are reported jointly (the former PMAK aggregate), which is why they appear as one line here; from 2017 they are counted separately. The shares refer to offences known to the police; this statistic says nothing about unreported crime.
en.BKA, Bundesweite Fallzahlen zur politisc: German Federal Criminal Police Office, national figures on politically motivated crime 2025 (fact sheet), series 2016–2025; own calculation of the shares.
en.Registrierte Fälle, aufgeklärte Fälle un: Recorded cases, cleared cases and convictions compared (different units and years — read as orders of magnitude).
en.Warum die Abstände nicht die Wirklichkei: Why the gaps do not reflect reality: the data show only what was reported to the police — and how the police count it. Eurostat itself points out that each country has its own criminal law, its own offence definitions and its own counting rules, and that the figures cover only cases that came to police attention. Willingness to report differs considerably: in Germany, the reporting rate for violent offences is usually below ten per cent according to the Federal Criminal Police Office's LeSuBiA dark-field study. For assault there is an additional German peculiarity: the offence of dangerous bodily harm under section 224 of the Criminal Code groups together cases that other countries partly count as simple assault. Germany's distance from the middle is therefore above all a picture of recording practice, not of the violence rate.
en.Die Häufigkeitszahl (Fälle je 100.000 Ei: Recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants vary by more than a factor of three between the federal states. The city-states lead by a wide margin — which also reflects commuters, tourists and different reporting practices, not only more crime.
en.Das Unsicherheitsgefühl folgt der Krimin: The feeling of being unsafe does not follow recorded crime. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has the lowest offence rate but the highest measured fear; Bavaria is low on both. The case numbers per state are small — pooled across six survey rounds, reported with intervals.
en.BIP je Einwohner und verfügbares Einkomm: GDP per capita and disposable income vary considerably. The city-states lead on GDP but sit closer to the middle on disposable income — because much value is created there, yet the cost of living is higher too.
en.Zwischen registrierten Fällen und Verurt: Between recorded cases and convictions lies a double selection: not every report is cleared, and not every cleared case leads to a conviction. The narrowing is strongest for burglary and theft.

en.Wie registrierte Fälle eines Delikts aus: How recorded cases of an offence end — as shares, so that all four offences sit on one scale: not cleared, cleared without conviction, convicted. The narrowing happens in two stages and varies widely: from 4.2 per cent of theft cases ending in conviction to 30 per cent for aggravated assault.
en.Einordnung: Von 1.813.141 registrierten: Reading: of 1,813,141 recorded thefts (2025), 577,495 were cleared (31.9 per cent); 75,740 convictions (2024) amount to 4.2 per cent of the cases. For residential burglary, 5,844 convictions stand against 82,920 cases (7.0 per cent), for robbery 6,098 against 40,119 (15.2 per cent), for aggravated assault 46,523 against 155,002 (30.0 per cent). Interpretation: both stages narrow the count, but independently — aggravated assault is cleared in 80.4 per cent of cases, yet only 30 per cent end in conviction; theft is cleared in 31.9 per cent and only 4.2 per cent lead to conviction. Anyone inferring a high number of convictions from a high clearance rate overlooks the second stage. Limits: the three quantities come from different sources and years — cases and clearances from the 2025 police crime statistics, convictions from the 2024 conviction statistics — and convictions count persons, not cases. Some 2024 convictions relate to cases from earlier years; for residential burglary the conviction figure covers only the aggravated forms under sections 243, 244 and 244a of the Criminal Code. The breakdown is therefore an approximation, not a balance of the same proceedings.

en.Kriminalität und Angst — Deutschland und: Crime and Fear — Germany and Switzerland
en.Deutschland und die Schweiz, dieselben F: Germany and Switzerland, the same questions: what gets recorded, what gets cleared — and how safe do people feel? The analyses draw on official police statistics, on the European Social Survey and on the victim surveys of both countries. Every figure carries its source, case count and limitation; correlations are labelled as correlations, not as causes.
en.Die Bundesrepublik und jedes Bundesland: The Federal Republic and each federal state
en.In beiden Ländern folgt das Sicherheitsg: In both countries the sense of safety does not follow recorded crime. In Germany the number of recorded offences has fallen by 18 per cent since 1993, while the share of people feeling unsafe in 2023 stood at 25.0 per cent, above its 2002 level. In Switzerland recorded crime has been practically flat since 2009, yet the share feeling unsafe fell from 16.1 to 8.9 per cent. Both findings rest on the same question in the same survey — and they contradict the assumption that fear simply follows crime.
What this does not say: why that is so. The pages document correlations, not causes. Anyone offering an explanation should be able to say which observation would refute it.
